introduction-not-putting-all-your-eggs-i.core: Multi-cloud means using more than one cloud provider. It can reduce dependence and meet regulatory or best-of-breed needs, but it multiplies complexity, cost and skills requirements, so it should be a deliberate strategy, not a default.

first_principles.problem: Leadership demands 'multi-cloud for resilience' without counting the cost of running everything twice.
truths: Each cloud has unique APIs and services.
Operating several platforms needs more expertise.
Benefits depend on the specific goals.
derivation: Clarify the **goal**: resilience, regulation, negotiation leverage, best-of-breed.

analogy.title: Keeping money in several banks
analogy.story: It reduces risk from one bank failing, but means more apps, statements and fees to manage.
analogy.breaks: Multi-cloud for resilience is rarely cheaper than multi-region on a single cloud.

example.title: Goals that justify multi-cloud
flow: Regulation: data must stay with a local provider

check.q: Why shouldn't multi-cloud be adopted by default?
check.a: It significantly increases complexity, cost and skill requirements, which only specific goals justify.

vendor-lock-in-analysis-the-hotel-califo.core: Lock-in is the cost of switching away. It comes from proprietary APIs, data gravity, contracts and skills. It isn't inherently bad: managed services trade lock-in for velocity. Analyse switching cost against the value each dependency provides.

first_principles.problem: Teams either avoid all managed services (slow) or adopt everything proprietary (trapped) without weighing the trade-off.
truths: Every dependency has a switching cost.
derivation: List **dependencies** by type: compute, data, proprietary services.
Accept lock-in **consciously** where the value exceeds the risk.

analogy.title: Hotel California
analogy.story: 'You can check out any time you like, but you can never leave.' Easy to enter, costly to exit.
analogy.breaks: The likelihood of switching matters too, since a low-probability exit doesn't justify heavy abstraction.

example.title: A lock-in assessment
flow: DynamoDB: high lock-in, high value → accept
Step Functions: medium → wrap with interface
S3: data gravity → plan exit path

check.a: No. Managed services can deliver value that outweighs the switching cost, so the key is to accept lock-in consciously.

abstraction-layers-the-universal-adapter.core: Portability needs abstraction layers: containers and Kubernetes for compute, Terraform or Crossplane for provisioning, open-source data stores and formats, and service-level interfaces. Each layer adds portability, and also complexity and a lowest-common-denominator effect.

first_principles.problem: Teams abstract everything 'for portability' and end up unable to use any provider's best features.
truths: Abstraction cuts access to unique features.
derivation: **Abstract selectively**: only where the switching likelihood justifies it.

analogy.title: Universal travel adapters
analogy.story: One adapter works in many countries, but you can't use the fast-charging feature of a specific socket.
analogy.breaks: Lowest-common-denominator designs give up real advantages.

example.title: A selective abstraction strategy
flow: Don't abstract: managed analytics where it's best-in-class
Interface: thin storage adapter for object stores

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Portability where it matters, power where it counts.

check.q: What's the 'lowest common denominator' problem in multi-cloud abstraction?
check.a: Abstracting across providers limits you to features they all share, giving up each one's best capabilities.

the-reality-check-data-gravity-and-exit-.core: Stateless compute moves easily between clouds; data doesn't. Large datasets, egress fees, replication lag and the services clustered around data (data gravity) make data the real lock-in. Exit strategies have to plan for data first.

first_principles.problem: A 'portable' Kubernetes app depends on 500 TB in S3 and a cloud-native database, so moving it is impractical.
truths: Data volume makes moves slow and costly.
derivation: **Document and test** the exit strategy (partial drills).

analogy.title: Moving house with a piano
analogy.story: Packing clothes is easy; the piano needs special movers, time and money.
analogy.breaks: Some providers now waive egress for full exits, so check current terms.

example.title: Estimating an exit
flow: Plan: dual-write new data, bulk transfer old
example.outcome: exit strategies grounded in data reality.

check.q: Why is data, not compute, usually the main obstacle to switching clouds?
check.a: Large datasets are slow and costly to move (egress, time), and dependent services cluster around them.

cost-arbitrage-the-elusive-dream.core: The idea of dynamically shifting workloads to the cheapest cloud rarely pays off. Egress fees, duplicated tooling, lost commitment discounts and operational complexity usually exceed the price differences, except for specific, portable batch workloads.

first_principles.problem: A 'cost arbitrage' strategy duplicates infrastructure across clouds and ends up costing more.
truths: Moving data between clouds is expensive.
Operating two platforms needs more staff.
derivation: Count the **total cost**: egress, tooling, people, lost discounts.
Compare it with the **real price differences**.
Arbitrage only **portable, data-light** workloads (batch compute, CI).

analogy.title: Driving across town for cheaper petrol
analogy.story: The fuel and time spent travelling cost more than you save.
analogy.breaks: GPU scarcity can justify multi-cloud capacity sourcing for ML.

check.q: Why does multi-cloud cost arbitrage usually fail?
check.a: Egress fees, duplicated tooling, staffing and lost volume discounts outweigh the price differences.

multi-cloud-patterns-that-actually-work.core: Practical multi-cloud patterns are: best-of-breed (each workload on the cloud best for it), segmented (different business units or acquisitions on different clouds), regulatory placement, and DR to a second cloud for critical systems. Full active-active portability everywhere rarely makes sense.

first_principles.problem: Teams attempt symmetric, everything-everywhere multi-cloud and drown in complexity.
truths: Different clouds excel at different things.
Critical systems may justify cross-cloud DR.
derivation: **Best-of-breed**: AWS core, GCP analytics, Azure for M365-integrated apps.
**Segmented**: per BU or acquisition, with a shared identity and governance layer.
**Cross-cloud DR** for the most critical systems; a **common control plane** (identity, policy, observability).

analogy.title: Using different shops for different needs
analogy.story: Groceries from the supermarket, tools from the hardware store, rather than buying everything from both.
analogy.breaks: Even pragmatic multi-cloud needs investment in a common control plane.

example.title: A pragmatic multi-cloud architecture
flow: GCP: BigQuery analytics via federated data
Common: Okta SSO, OPA policies, Datadog, FOCUS billing

check.q: What's a common, practical multi-cloud pattern?
check.a: Best-of-breed: placing each workload on the cloud that serves it best, with a shared identity and governance layer.
